blocks.prompt: The Guinea Pig That Is Not a Pig
blocks.text: A guinea pig is not a pig. It is also not from a place called Guinea. So the name is wrong twice. A guinea pig comes from the high mountains of South America, in a country called Peru. Guinea pigs eat grass and hay all day long. They have to. Their teeth never stop growing, and chewing tough grass keeps the teeth short. A guinea pig hops in the air when it feels good. People call that popcorning. A guinea pig also whistles when it is hungry. It looks for you, and it whistles until you come.

blocks.prompt: The Animal With Two Wrong Names
blocks.text: The guinea pig is not a pig, and it has never lived in Guinea. Scientists call it a cavy, and it belongs to a family of rodents from South America. Its home is the Andes, a long chain of cold, high mountains running down the western edge of the continent. People there have kept cavies for thousands of years, long before anyone in Europe had heard of them. So where did the silly name come from? Nobody is certain. Sailors may have carried the animals on ships that stopped in Guinea, in Africa, on the way to Europe. The pig part is easier. The animal is round, it squeals, and it spends almost all day eating. A guinea pig has to eat almost all day. Its teeth keep growing for its whole life, the way your fingernails do, and only hours of chewing tough grass grinds them back down. If a guinea pig stops chewing, its teeth become too long to eat with.

blocks.prompt: The Whistle That Was Made For Us
blocks.text: Guinea pigs are not wild animals that people tamed last week. They are one of the oldest domesticated animals on Earth. In the high valleys of the Andes, farmers began keeping cavies around seven thousand years ago, penning them beside the cooking fire and feeding them kitchen scraps. Over all those centuries the animal changed. It grew rounder, calmer, and more colorful than its wild cousins, which are lean, gray, and hard to catch. Domestication left one strange gift behind. Guinea pigs make a piercing whistle, a sound keepers call wheeking, and they mostly aim it at people. Wild cavies do not greet each other this way. A pet guinea pig learns the rattle of a bag, the creak of a door, the footsteps of the person who brings the food, and it whistles at that sound and nothing else. It is not talking to other guinea pigs. It is talking to you. Domestication also left a weakness. Guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C. Almost every other mammal builds vitamin C inside its body, but somewhere in the guinea pig's past that ability broke, and it never came back. Humans have exactly the same fault. That is why sailors once got scurvy at sea, and it is why a pet guinea pig fed only dry pellets will sicken. It needs fresh food, every single day, for the same reason you do. Their babies are strange too. Most rodents are born pink, blind, and helpless. A newborn guinea pig arrives with a full coat of fur, open eyes, a working set of teeth, and it can run within a few hours of being born.

blocks.prompt: How a Small Rodent Became a Figure of Speech
blocks.text: When you say someone is a guinea pig, you mean they are the one the experiment is being tried on. That phrase is about four hundred years old, and the animal earned it honestly. In 1780 the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier wanted to answer a question nobody had answered: is the warmth of a living body a kind of burning? He built a device with an inner chamber packed in ice, placed a guinea pig inside, and measured how much ice the animal's body heat melted. Then he measured the carbon dioxide it breathed out. The numbers lined up. Life, he concluded, is a slow fire. That experiment helped begin the science of how bodies turn food into energy, and a guinea pig was sitting at the center of it. Cavies kept appearing in laboratories for a reason that has nothing to do with luck. They are small, calm, and easy to keep. More importantly, they are broken in the same particular way we are. Almost every mammal manufactures its own vitamin C. Guinea pigs cannot, because the gene that builds the necessary enzyme is present in their DNA but permanently switched off. Primates, including humans, carry the identical fault. That shared weakness made the guinea pig the animal that finally proved scurvy is a deficiency and not an infection, and it is why vitamin C was isolated using guinea pigs in the 1930s. The oldest chapter of the story is not scientific at all. Long before Europeans met them, cavies were livestock. Andean families kept them loose in the kitchen, where they ate scraps and warmed themselves near the fire, and where they were also eaten. That has not changed. Peruvians still eat tens of millions of guinea pigs a year, a dish called cuy, and it is served at weddings and festivals rather than at ordinary dinners. In the cathedral at Cusco there is a painting of the Last Supper by an Andean artist named Marcos Zapata. The apostles are gathered around the table. Laid out on the platter in front of them, roasted and whole, is a guinea pig. Depending on where you stand on the planet, the same animal is a pet you buy hay for, a laboratory subject in a photograph, or the meal at a celebration. The animal has not changed. Only the people looking at it have.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Cavia porcellus, domesticated from a wild Andean cavy
Kept by Andean households roughly 7,000 years
GULO gene present but permanently inactivated
Lavoisier's 1780 ice calorimeter used a guinea pig
Gestation 59 to 72 days, very long for a rodent
Swiss law forbids keeping a single guinea pig alone

blocks.prompt: A Broken Gene, a Slow Fire, and a Painting in Cusco
blocks.text: The guinea pig is misnamed twice over. It is not a pig, and no part of its history touches Guinea. It is a cavy, a South American rodent, and its story is worth more than the joke about its name, because this small animal sits at the intersection of three things that rarely meet: a genetic accident, the birth of modern chemistry, and a question about who gets to decide what an animal is for. Start with the accident. Nearly every mammal manufactures its own vitamin C in the liver, using an enzyme built by a gene called GULO. Guinea pigs do not. The gene is still there in their DNA, sitting in the correct place on the correct chromosome, but it is a ruin. Mutations have accumulated in it until it no longer produces anything, and no repair ever came. Primates, our own species included, carry a version of the same ruin, broken independently and long ago. This is not a coincidence so much as a permission. An animal whose diet is drowning in fresh vitamin C has no reason to spend energy manufacturing it, so when the gene failed, nothing punished the failure and it was passed on. The consequence is that guinea pigs, almost uniquely among laboratory animals, can get scurvy. That single shared flaw made them the animal on which scurvy was proven to be a deficiency rather than an infection, and the animal in which vitamin C was finally hunted down and isolated in the 1930s. Now the chemistry. In 1780 Antoine Lavoisier was pursuing a question that sounds childish and was not: is being alive a form of burning? He built an ice calorimeter, an inner chamber surrounded by packed ice, and placed a guinea pig in it. He measured the meltwater the animal's body heat produced, then measured the carbon dioxide it exhaled, and compared both against what happened when he burned charcoal in the same apparatus. The ratios corresponded. Respiration, he concluded, is combustion, running slowly and coolly inside the body. That result is the foundation of everything we understand about metabolism, and the subject of the experiment was a rodent that had been sitting in Andean kitchens for millennia. Which brings the last thread. Cavies were domesticated in the Andes around seven thousand years ago, before the llama, and they were not pets. They were livestock, kept loose indoors, fed on scraps, and eaten. They still are. Peru consumes tens of millions of guinea pigs a year as cuy, reserved for weddings and festivals rather than weeknights. In the cathedral at Cusco hangs a Last Supper painted by Marcos Zapata, an Andean artist working in the 1750s. The apostles lean toward the table, and on the central platter, roasted and unmistakable, lies a guinea pig. Zapata was painting the most sacred meal he could imagine, so he painted the food a feast is actually made of. Here is what makes the animal genuinely interesting. Nothing about the guinea pig changes across these three stories. The same creature is a broken gene, a measuring instrument, a sacred meal, and a child's first pet, and it is all of them simultaneously. What changes is the person deciding. We tend to imagine those categories are properties of the animal, the way fur and teeth are. They are not. They are properties of us.
